title: AfterDrink Review: Does It Work? 25 Ingredients, DHM Dose and Value
excerpt: An honest AfterDrink review: what a 25-ingredient formula means for each dose, how its DHM compares with standalone DHM, side effects, user sentiment, and who it suits.
metaDescription: Honest AfterDrink review: what its 25-ingredient formula means for each dose, DHM vs standalone DHM, side effects, user reviews, and who it suits.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest verdict first:** AfterDrink is a capsule hangover supplement built on the "kitchen sink" idea: roughly two dozen vitamins, minerals, amino acids, and herbal extracts in one serving, with DHM (dihydromyricetin, a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree) as one of them. Plenty of buyers say it helps them feel better the next morning, and the broad formula is the main selling point. But no large independent trial has tested AfterDrink itself, and the long ingredient list comes with a trade-off most reviews skip: when you split a few capsules' worth of powder across around 25 ingredients, each one ends up at a small dose. That includes DHM, which is present at a fraction of what standalone DHM products deliver.

**Who it suits:** occasional social drinkers who like the idea of one broad "cover the bases" product and don't need any single ingredient at a high dose. **Who should skip it:** people who mainly want DHM (a plain DHM product gives you far more per serving), people on several prescription medicines (more herbs means more interaction questions), people with sensitive stomachs, and anyone drinking heavily or often, which no supplement fixes.

> **This is not medical advice.** This review explains published research, the brand's own descriptions, and general supplement science. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. AfterDrink is a dietary supplement, not a drug. It has not been approved by the FDA to prevent or treat hangovers, and it does not lower your blood alcohol, sober you up, or make it safe to drive. **Ask a doctor or pharmacist first if** you take prescription medicine (especially blood thinners, diabetes medicines, sedatives, sleep aids, or anxiety medication), are pregnant or breastfeeding, or have liver or kidney disease. If someone shows signs of alcohol poisoning, such as confusion, vomiting while drowsy, slow or irregular breathing, or can't be woken up, call 911.

**About our relationship with AfterDrink:** we don't have an affiliate arrangement with AfterDrink, so this review doesn't link to their store and we earn nothing if you buy it. We do earn a commission on two plain DHM products mentioned near the end, and we say so where they appear.

## What AfterDrink Is

AfterDrink is a hangover supplement sold in capsule form online and through large retailers. Its marketing leans on breadth: rather than betting on one or two ingredients, it packs in a long list of nutrients and botanicals that each have some connection, strong or weak, to alcohol metabolism, hydration, or how you feel the next day. Depending on the version and the listing, you'll see the formula described as having around 25 ingredients.

Those ingredients generally fall into a few groups:

- **B vitamins** such as thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2), niacin (B3), B6, and B12. Alcohol use can lower some B vitamin levels, which is the usual reason they appear in hangover formulas.
- **Vitamin C and other antioxidants**, pitched as helping with the oxidative stress (cell wear and tear from reactive molecules) that alcohol metabolism creates.
- **Minerals and electrolytes** such as magnesium, zinc, and potassium, aimed at what you lose through more frequent urination while drinking.
- **Amino acids** such as cysteine-type compounds, which feed into your body's own antioxidant called glutathione.
- **Herbal extracts**, which across hangover formulas typically include things like milk thistle, prickly pear, ginger, ginseng, and similar botanicals.
- **DHM**, the ingredient most associated with hangover supplements today.

One honest caution before we go further: the exact ingredient list and the amounts have not been reported the same way everywhere over the years, and formulas get reworked. We're not going to quote precise milligram figures we can't confirm for the version you'll find on the shelf. Instead, this review focuses on the thing you can check yourself in ten seconds, which is the Supplement Facts panel, and on what the overall design of the formula means for you.

## The Kitchen-Sink Problem: What 25 Ingredients Means for Each Dose

This is the most important section of the review, because it applies to AfterDrink and to every product built the same way.

A capsule has a physical size limit. A standard large capsule (the "00" size used by most supplements) holds somewhere around 500 to 800 mg of powder, depending on how dense the powder is. Most hangover supplements ask you to take a few capsules per serving. That means a full serving usually contains, at most, a couple of grams of total material, and some of that is filler, flow agents, and the capsule shell itself.

Now divide that by about 25 ingredients. Even if every ingredient got an equal share, which they don't, the average comes out well under 100 mg each. In practice, some ingredients take up much more room than others (minerals like magnesium are bulky), so others get squeezed down to very small amounts.

Here's why that matters. The research on hangover ingredients, thin as it is, was done at specific doses. When a study finds something promising at, say, 1,000 mg, that tells you very little about whether 50 mg will do anything. A long ingredient list looks impressive on the front of a bottle, but it can mean you're getting a sprinkle of many things rather than a meaningful amount of any one.

**How to check this yourself:** look at the Supplement Facts panel. Ingredients listed with their own milligram amount tell you exactly what you're getting. Ingredients grouped under a "proprietary blend" only show the total weight of the blend, not each ingredient. US rules require blend ingredients to be listed in descending order by weight, so anything near the end of a blend list is present in the smallest amounts. If DHM sits inside a blend, you can't know its dose, only that it's less than the blend total.

This isn't a claim that AfterDrink is dishonest. It's a design choice. Broad formulas trade dose for variety, and some people genuinely prefer that. You just deserve to know the trade-off before you pay for it.

## DHM Dose: AfterDrink vs Standalone DHM

DHM is the ingredient most people are looking for when they buy a hangover supplement, so it's worth comparing directly.

Standalone DHM supplements typically provide between 300 mg and 1,000 mg per serving. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains where those numbers come from: most of the research is in animals, the human evidence is limited, and products commonly land at 300 mg to 1,200 mg for an evening of drinking, scaled roughly to how much you plan to drink and to body weight.

In a formula with around 25 ingredients, DHM has to share the same capsule space as everything else. Whatever the exact figure on the version you buy, it will be a fraction of the standalone range. That doesn't mean it does nothing. We simply don't have good evidence about what DHM does at low doses in people, and the reasonable assumption is that more of the ingredient you care about gives you a better chance of an effect.

| | AfterDrink-style broad formula | Standalone DHM supplement |
|---|---|---|
| **DHM per serving** | A fraction of the standalone range (check the label) | Usually 300 mg to 1,000 mg |
| **Number of ingredients** | Around 25 | One, or a few |
| **What you're paying for** | Variety and convenience | A higher dose of one ingredient |
| **Interaction checking** | Harder (many herbs) | Easier (one ingredient) |
| **Stomach upset risk** | Somewhat higher with more botanicals and B vitamins | Generally low |

If DHM is your main interest, a plain DHM product is the more direct route. If you want DHM plus a broad mix of vitamins and herbs and you're comfortable with the smaller doses, a product like AfterDrink is built for exactly that.

## Does AfterDrink Work? The Ingredient Evidence

There are no published independent clinical trials of AfterDrink as a finished product that we're aware of. So the honest way to answer "does it work?" is to look at the evidence for its main ingredients, then ask whether the doses in the formula are likely to match the doses that were studied.

### DHM: promising, mostly from animal research

The best-known DHM study is a 2012 paper in the *Journal of Neuroscience* by Shen and colleagues. In rats, DHM reduced signs of alcohol intoxication and withdrawal, apparently by acting on GABA-A receptors, the brain receptors that alcohol also affects. Other lab and animal research suggests DHM may support the enzymes that clear alcohol and its toxic by-product acetaldehyde, and may have antioxidant effects in the liver.

The weak point is human evidence. Good placebo-controlled hangover trials of DHM in people are scarce, and DHM is also known to be poorly absorbed when taken by mouth. Our [honest review of whether DHM works](/never-hungover/does-dhm-work-honest-science-review-2025) goes through this in detail. The short of it: promising, plausible, not proven, and studied mostly at doses higher than what a crowded formula can fit.

### Cysteine-type amino acids: one small human trial

A 2020 randomized, placebo-controlled study in *Alcohol and Alcoholism* (Eriksson and colleagues, in Finland) tested L-cysteine in a small group of men and reported less nausea and headache after drinking compared with placebo in some measures. Cysteine helps the body make glutathione, which is part of how you neutralize acetaldehyde. It's a real result, but a small one from a single trial, and it hasn't been widely repeated. If a version of AfterDrink includes cysteine or N-acetyl cysteine, the same dose question applies. Our [NAC vs DHM comparison](/never-hungover/nac-vs-dhm-which-antioxidant-better-liver-protection-2025) covers this group of ingredients in more depth.

### Prickly pear: a modest signal from 2004

A 2004 study in the *Archives of Internal Medicine* (Wiese and colleagues) found that an extract of prickly pear cactus, taken before drinking, reduced some hangover symptoms such as nausea and dry mouth in a small group of volunteers, though it didn't reduce overall hangover severity on every measure. It's one of the few herbal hangover ingredients with a human trial behind it. We compare it head to head in [DHM vs prickly pear](/never-hungover/dhm-vs-prickly-pear-hangovers).

### Milk thistle, ginger, ginseng, and other botanicals

These are common in broad hangover formulas. Milk thistle (silymarin) is studied mainly for liver conditions, not hangovers. Ginger has reasonable evidence for nausea in other settings, such as pregnancy and motion sickness, which is why it shows up here. Some small studies have looked at red ginseng and alcohol, but the evidence is limited. None of these has strong evidence as a hangover remedy on its own, and all of them were studied at doses that a 25-ingredient formula may not reach. Our [DHM vs milk thistle comparison](/never-hungover/dhm-vs-milk-thistle-which-liver-supplement-more-effective-2025) explains what milk thistle can and can't do.

### Vitamins and electrolytes

B vitamins, vitamin C, and electrolytes are cheap, safe at normal doses, and make sense on paper. But dehydration is only one part of a hangover, and research on hangovers (for example, work by Penning and colleagues published around 2010) has found that how hydrated people are doesn't line up neatly with how bad their hangover feels. Researchers increasingly see hangovers as driven mainly by the immune system's inflammatory response and by acetaldehyde, with poor sleep and low blood sugar adding to it. Vitamins and electrolytes may help you feel a little better; they're unlikely to be the main event.

### What the bigger reviews say

When researchers have pooled the hangover remedy studies, the picture has been consistently underwhelming. A 2005 systematic review in the *BMJ* (Pittler, Verster, and Ernst) concluded there was no compelling evidence that any conventional or complementary remedy prevents or treats hangovers. A later systematic review in *Addiction* (Jayawardena and colleagues, 2017) found a handful of promising candidates but judged the overall evidence to be low quality. That's the backdrop for every hangover supplement, AfterDrink included.

### Does the combination add up?

This is the honest heart of the kitchen-sink question. The theory behind broad formulas is that many small doses of different ingredients add up to more than any one alone. That's possible, but it hasn't been demonstrated. No one has run a trial showing that 25 ingredients at low doses outperform, say, a full dose of one or two well-chosen ingredients. It's equally possible that most of the ingredients are present at levels too low to matter, and that any benefit people notice comes from a few of them, or from drinking water with the capsules, or from expecting to feel better.

### What AfterDrink can't do

No supplement, including this one:

- Lowers your blood alcohol or makes you sober faster
- Makes it safe to drive
- Protects you from the damage of regular heavy drinking
- Prevents alcohol poisoning

If you notice that taking a supplement makes you comfortable drinking more than you otherwise would, that's a net loss.

## AfterDrink Side Effects and Safety

### Possible side effects

Most buyers don't report problems. The complaints that come up with broad hangover formulas, AfterDrink included, tend to be:

- **Stomach upset or nausea**, especially when taken on an empty stomach or with a lot of alcohol already on board
- **Flushing, warmth, or tingling**, which can happen with niacin (vitamin B3)
- **Bright yellow urine**, which is harmless and comes from riboflavin (B2)
- **Headache or a "buzzy" feeling** in a minority of people
- **Allergic reactions**, which are rare but more possible when a product contains many plant extracts

### Medication interactions

This is where a 25-ingredient formula needs more caution than a single-ingredient one. Every herbal extract is a separate thing to check against your medications. A few examples of the kinds of concerns pharmacists look for:

- **Blood thinners** such as warfarin: some herbs, including ginger and ginseng, may affect bleeding or how these drugs work.
- **Diabetes medicines**: some botanicals, including prickly pear and ginseng, may lower blood sugar, and alcohol already affects blood sugar.
- **Drugs processed by liver enzymes**: milk thistle and some other herbs may affect liver enzymes that break down many prescription medicines.
- **Sedatives, sleep aids, and anxiety medication**: DHM appears to act on the same brain receptors as these drugs and alcohol, so combining them deserves a conversation with a doctor.

Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers the DHM side in detail. For the full AfterDrink formula, the simplest approach is to take the bottle, or a photo of the label, to a pharmacist and ask.

### Who should avoid it or ask first

- People who are pregnant or breastfeeding (there's no safety data for this kind of formula)
- People with liver or kidney disease
- Anyone taking prescription medicine, especially the types listed above
- People with known allergies to plants in the daisy family, which includes milk thistle
- Anyone under 21, or anyone who shouldn't be drinking at all

Also be careful about painkillers. Taking acetaminophen (Tylenol) on top of heavy drinking has its own serious liver risks, which we explain in our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol). A supplement doesn't change those rules.

## What Users Say About AfterDrink

User reviews on retailer sites and forums are mixed in a way that's typical for hangover supplements. Reviews aren't clinical evidence, and people who have a strong reaction either way are the most likely to write one, but patterns are still useful.

### What people like

- **"I felt more normal the next day."** This is the most common positive comment, usually from people who took it with water after a night out.
- **Convenience.** People like having one product rather than juggling several.
- **The broad formula.** Some buyers specifically like that it includes vitamins and electrolytes along with herbal ingredients.

### What people complain about

- **No noticeable effect.** A meaningful share of reviewers say they felt no different, especially after heavier nights.
- **Number of capsules.** Broad formulas often need several capsules per serving, which some people find hard to swallow late at night.
- **Stomach upset.** A minority mention nausea, especially when taken on an empty stomach.
- **Cost per serving.** Some reviewers note that the price adds up quickly if you drink often.

### The recurring advice from experienced users

Across hangover supplement discussions generally, the same advice shows up again and again: the products seem to work best for moderate nights, they work better alongside water, food, and sleep, and they don't rescue a night of very heavy drinking. That matches what the research would predict.

## Pricing and Value

We don't quote exact prices here because they change often and vary by retailer and pack size. The useful way to judge value is cost per serving compared with what you're actually getting.

### The value verdict

If you're buying AfterDrink for its breadth, the price is in the normal range for multi-ingredient hangover supplements. If you're buying it mainly for DHM, the value is weaker, because you're paying for a long list of other ingredients and getting a smaller DHM dose than a cheaper standalone product would give you.

A useful exercise: divide the price of a bottle by the number of servings, then look at how much DHM each serving contains. Do the same for a plain DHM product. In our experience, the standalone products almost always win on DHM per dollar, often by a wide margin.

### Cheaper DHM alternatives

If DHM is what you're after, these are two standalone options we've reviewed:

- [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20): about 1,000 mg of DHM plus L-cysteine and a few supporting ingredients, so it sits between a plain DHM product and a broad formula. It costs more per serving than Double Wood.

Neither is a proven hangover cure either. They simply give you more of the ingredient most people are paying for. You can compare more options on our [supplement reviews page](/reviews).

## How AfterDrink Compares With Other Hangover Products

The hangover supplement market splits into a few camps, and it helps to know where AfterDrink sits:

- **Broad formulas** (AfterDrink and similar): many ingredients, small dose of each. Good for people who value coverage over dose.
- **DHM-focused formulas** such as Cheers Restore: DHM plus a few supporting ingredients. Our [Cheers Restore review](/never-hungover/cheers-restore-review) explains the trade-offs there.
- **Plain DHM products**: the highest DHM dose for the money and the simplest label.
- **Probiotic drinks** such as ZBiotics, which work on a different idea (an engineered bacterium that breaks down acetaldehyde in the gut). See our [ZBiotics review](/never-hungover/zbiotics-review).
- **Hangover patches**, which have even less evidence behind them. We look at those in [do hangover patches work](/never-hungover/do-hangover-patches-work).

Other brands in the broad-formula and drink-mix space include Flyby, More Labs, Liverite, and others. Our [Flyby Recovery review](/never-hungover/flyby-recovery-review-2025) is a good comparison if you're weighing two broad formulas against each other, and our [complete guide to hangover supplements](/never-hungover/hangover-supplements-complete-guide-what-actually-works-2025) puts all of these categories side by side.

## How to Use AfterDrink (If You Try It)

If you decide to try it, a few habits give you the best chance of a good result and the lowest chance of a bad one:

1. **Read the label first.** Check the serving size, the DHM amount if listed, and every herbal ingredient against your medications.
2. **Follow the label directions.** Don't double the dose to "make up" for a heavy night.
3. **Take it with a full glass of water.** Some of the benefit people notice may simply come from drinking water before bed.
4. **Eat something.** Food slows alcohol absorption and makes stomach upset less likely.
5. **Try it on a moderate night first.** That way you'll know whether it agrees with you before you rely on it.
6. **Keep the basics in place.** Pace yourself, alternate with water, and protect your sleep. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers what makes the biggest difference.

## Pros and Cons Summary

**Pros**

- Broad formula covering vitamins, minerals, amino acids, herbs, and DHM in one product
- Convenient for people who don't want to stack several supplements
- Some ingredients have small human studies behind them (prickly pear, cysteine)
- Plenty of users report feeling better the next morning

**Cons**

- No independent clinical trial of the finished product
- Around 25 ingredients means a small dose of each, including DHM
- Less DHM per serving and per dollar than standalone DHM products
- More herbal ingredients means more to check for medication interactions
- Several capsules per serving for many versions
- Formula details and amounts have varied between versions and listings

## The Bottom Line

AfterDrink is a reasonable product for people who want a broad, all-in-one approach and understand what that means: lots of ingredients, a small amount of each. It isn't a scam, and it isn't a proven cure. If you try it, read the label, check it against your medications, take it with water and food, and judge it on a moderate night.

If what you really want is DHM, you'll usually get much more of it, for less money, from a standalone product dosed according to our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025). And whatever you take, the things that matter most are still the unglamorous ones: drinking less, drinking slower, eating, drinking water, and sleeping.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does AfterDrink actually work?**

It may help some people feel a bit better, but it isn't proven. There's no large independent clinical trial of AfterDrink itself. A few of its ingredients, such as DHM, prickly pear, and L-cysteine type amino acids, have small or early-stage research behind them, but a formula with around 25 ingredients can only hold a modest amount of each one. User reviews are mixed: some people swear by it, others notice no difference. It does not lower your blood alcohol or make heavy drinking safe.

**How much DHM is in AfterDrink?**

AfterDrink lists DHM as one of many ingredients, and the exact amount has varied between versions and retailer listings, so check the label on the bottle you buy. The key point is simple math: a serving of a few capsules can only hold a couple of grams of powder in total, split across roughly two dozen ingredients. That leaves DHM well below the 300 mg to 1,000 mg that standalone DHM products typically provide per serving.

**Is AfterDrink better than plain DHM?**

Not necessarily. AfterDrink's appeal is variety: vitamins, minerals, herbs, and DHM in one product. If DHM is the ingredient you care about, a standalone DHM supplement gives you a much larger dose per serving, usually for less money. If you want broad coverage and don't mind smaller amounts of each ingredient, AfterDrink's approach may suit you. Neither is a proven hangover cure.

**When should I take AfterDrink?**

Follow the directions on the label. Like most multi-ingredient hangover supplements, it is generally marketed for use around drinking, either during or right after, with water. Taking it with food may reduce stomach upset. Don't take more than the label says, and don't take it as a reason to drink more.

**Does AfterDrink have side effects?**

Most people report no problems, but side effects are possible with any multi-ingredient supplement. The most common complaints with this type of product are stomach upset, nausea, and occasionally headache or flushing from B vitamins such as niacin. Because the formula contains many herbal extracts, the chance of an allergy or medication interaction is higher than with a single-ingredient product. Talk to a doctor or pharmacist first if you take prescription medicine, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or have liver or kidney disease.

**Can I take AfterDrink with other medications?**

Check with a doctor or pharmacist first. AfterDrink contains several herbal ingredients, and herbs such as milk thistle, ginseng, and others can interact with prescription drugs including blood thinners, diabetes medicines, and drugs processed by liver enzymes. DHM may also affect GABA receptors in the brain, so caution is sensible with sedatives, sleep aids, and anxiety medication. Bring the bottle or a photo of the label so they can see the full ingredient list.

**Is AfterDrink worth the money?**

It depends on what you value. If you like the idea of one product covering many bases and the price fits your budget, it's a reasonable choice to try. If you're paying mainly for the DHM, you'll usually get more DHM per dollar from a plain DHM supplement. Either way, the biggest hangover factors are still how much you drink, how fast, whether you eat, and how well you sleep.
